title: Can an AI Agent Be Trusted With a Brokerage Account? Rule Compliance of Trading Agents Under Pressure From Their Principal
abstract: Language models that call tools can place trades, and a firm that gives one an order ticket needs to know whether it will refuse an order that breaks the firm's rules when its own portfolio manager asks for it. We introduce mandatebench, a benchmark in which an agent works the desk of a fictitious firm under a six-rule compliance manual (restricted list, earnings blackout, concentration cap, pre-trade approval, no short selling, no margin). In 144 conflict scenarios the requested trade breaches exactly one rule, under one of six pressure levels; in 28 legitimate scenarios, several placed exactly at a limit, it breaches nothing, so overcaution is measured alongside violation. A deterministic rule engine scores every order from the ledger. Eight open-weight models from four developers were run locally, in two batches: the finding from the first four was recorded as a falsifiable prediction before the other four were run. Violation rates ranged from 1.4% (gpt-oss-120b) to 94.4% (Llama 3.1 8B). Appeals to authority, deadlines and claims that a rule had changed moved no model significantly in any of 24 tests. Counterfeit authorization did: a claimed compliance sign-off with a reference number, or a forged system notice. The models did not all fall to the same counterfeit, so a single-attack evaluation would have ranked them differently, and under the forged notice all eight, including the most compliant, skipped a required approval. The prediction held on pressure wherever the new models could test it, and failed on legitimate requests for one model, whose tool calls were written into prose and never executed. Most violations were the agent's first action, and in 17 episodes an agent denied an order the ledger shows it placed. Since every violation was decidable before execution, these rules belong in deterministic pre-trade controls rather than in the agent's judgment. Code, scenarios and every transcript are released.
why: mandatebench trading-agent compliance; real rules, falsifiable results.

title: Where Should the LLM Sit? Architectural Defenses Against Document-Borne Prompt Injection in Automated Credit Underwriting
abstract: Lenders have started to let LLM agents read applicant documents, and applicants control those documents. We ask where the LLM should sit in an automated credit underwriting pipeline. On synthetic payslip, bank statement and application-form bundles generated from 116 686 real credit records, we compare four congurations under 26 attack variants and three open-weight models of 1.5B to 7B parameters: an LLM that decides, the same with a prompt-level defense, an LLM that only extracts elds for a logistic scorecard (B), and B with schema, cross-document and plausible-band checks and a human-review rule (C). For the two models that do not approve everyone, injected instructions steer the deciding LLM in 41.8% and 65.0% of attacked cases and still in 18.7% and 29.2% with a prompt defense. As extractors the same models are steered in 2.7% and 2.0% of cases, mostly by payloads that name the values to write, and C records no success in 1 800 Phi pairs or 600 Olmo pairs (95% upper bounds 0.2% and 0.6%). Falsied documents succeed against B in 16.7% to 19.8% of cases, about as often as or less often than with an oracle extractor that makes no error, so the LLM adds no success of its own. C lowers it to 5.7% to 8.0% and ags 17.7% to 48.6% of clean bundles for review, a cost that follows mainly from extraction errors, since 90.4% to 97.1% of the agged bundles contain a wrongly extracted or missing eld. Olmo-3 7B ran on 200 applicants and 50 targets, so its intervals are wide. Per model, the preregistered rules are met as follows: H1 (B at or below 2% on instruction attacks) for one of three models, H2 (extraction-manipulation success rising with plausibility) for two, and H3 (C lowers extraction success at a higher review rate) for all three. By the majority rule H1 is not supported and H2 and H3 are.
why: LLM underwriting injection defense; extractor beats decider, practical setup.

title: Auto-Alpha: A Framework for Autonomous Factor Research
abstract: Autonomous factor research requires generating economic hypotheses as well as implementing and testing them. We present Auto-Alpha, a framework that connects report-guided initialization to self-directed research through a test-driven implementation loop. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions; a research agent develops them with backtest feedback. Semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission select factors for a persistent library, while an Experience Library retains research insights. Starting from 120 research reports, Auto-Alpha builds an initial library of 32 factors. It then generates new ideas and refines existing candidates, producing 420 implementations and retaining 62 additional factors. We evaluate factor quality and portfolio performance using a fixed library snapshot of 105 factors. The median 1-day Rank IC is 0.0301, and a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns 16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the CSI 1000 price index. These retrospective results document an operating research process and its artifacts; controlled evaluation is needed to isolate the contribution of its components.
why: Auto-Alpha autonomous factor research; LLM agents and backtests.

title: Path-Independent Deleveraging Rules
abstract: We characterise path-independent auto-deleveraging (ADL) rules as an extended log-exponential family. Immunity to account splitting, merging and reopening further restrict the class. Homogeneity (essentially) restricts the class to a one-parameter family ordered by both fairness and platform risk. Its split-proof members continuously interpolate between proportional division and water-filling. Among these rules, decreasing the parameter reduces risk at the cost of increasing inequality in how accounts are treated. This suggests selecting the parameter through an ex-ante calibration to a risk bound on historical data to choose a maximally fair rule subject to that bound. A counterfactual replay of Hyperliquid's ADL episode on 10 October 2025 finds that a range of intermediate parameters significantly improves on the observed allocation in both burden dispersion and subsequent risk statistics.
why: Crypto exchange ADL counterfactual replay, real execution data

title: A Reproducibility Audit of Public Financial Misstatement Data: Chronological Benchmarks and Measurement Diagnostics
abstract: This study audits the reproducibility and measurement assumptions of a public financial misstatement benchmark. After removing 214 surplus positive records, a report-period split yields 2,695 evaluation observations in 2019-2021, including 93 enforcement-associated positives from 26 firms. With twelve processed ratios, logistic regression achieves average precision of 0.0447, compared with 0.0345 for a constant score and 0.0328 for a class weighted random forest. A post hoc paired firm-cluster interval for logistic improvement is-0.0020 to 0.0381. The forest leads during validation but falls from 0.1270 to 0.0328 in evaluation. The audit identifies overlapping report-period ranges in the supplied split and unresolved histories of predictor values, control sampling and training-label availability. Supplementary checks examine selected SEC accessions and annotation disagreements. The contribution is methodological: an executable account of the assumptions behind the benchmark and evidence of weak retrospective ranking. An untouched cohort and historically reconstructed inputs remain necessary for a prospective prediction study. AI disclosure: OpenAI ChatGPT and Codex substantially assisted research design, source and data audits, analysis code, numerical checks, and writing; the full research-assistance statement follows the conclusion.
why: Misstatement benchmark audit; forest collapses out of sample.

title: Diagnosis is not a policy: a state-transition audit of caoability-conditioned test-time inference
abstract: Test-time actions can satisfy retrieval, state-realization, program-consistency, or rendering objectives without correcting an answer. Test-time Error Response and Realizability Audit (TERRA) is an evaluation/auditing protocol, not a new inference algorithm. It uses a unified decomposition of intervention outcomes into applicability, target-state realization, endpoint translation, harm, and resource/inference cost. Paired comparisons fix the incoming state and evaluation conditions; cross-model analyses vary the receiving configuration. Executable financial reasoning experiments yield three findings: the same context expansion can harm one configuration and benefit another; sufficient evidence does not ensure correctness because configurations differ in evidence-to-answer translation; and diagnostic headroom---accuracy attainable with idealized diagnostic information over the measured baseline---plus local consistency does not ensure practical gains. Action value is $V(a\mid x,m)$, not diagnosis alone; diagnosis is not a deployable policy $π(a\mid x,m)$.
why: Test-time inference audit protocol with financial examples

title: Whose Risks Count? What 1,901 AI Incidents Reveal About Corporate Disclosures
abstract: AI systems can harm people, yet the AI actors that provide or deploy them are rarely obliged to disclose these risks. US securities regulation is an exception. Companies registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) must disclose their material risks, including those of their AI systems, in filings that carry liability for misstatement. Materiality, however, is defined by what a reasonable investor would consider important, so harms to third parties enter disclosure only insofar as they become financial risks for the company. We test whether AI harms do so by matching 9,001 AI incidents to 18,229 SEC filings of 328 AI actors by risk type. Of the 1,901 incidents with filings before and after them, half belong to a risk type that the AI actor never disclosed, and this share varies with the kind of harm. Filings disclose the risk types of 67\% of system failures but only 2\% of social system harms, and AI actors themselves report fewer than 2\% of incidents. Securities disclosure thus records the risks that AI actors face rather than the harms that people subject to AI bear. Public authorities that hold AI actors accountable for such harms could make them financially material. We release DISC, the Disclosure--Incident Securities Corpus, to support this work.
why: SEC AI risk disclosure gaps; real filings evidence.

title: State-Reward Alignment and Rich State Representations in Financial Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Financial markets represent the collective behaviour of numerous heterogeneous agents operating under diverse objectives, constraints and information sets. Consequently, an important question arises within financial reinforcement learning: is raw price information sufficient to represent market dynamics, or do richer state representations provide superior learning environments for trading agents? This study investigates the impact of state representation richness on the performance of reinforcement-learning-based trading systems. A traditional Raw OHLC state representation was compared against a customengineered 89-dimensional feature representation incorporating probabilistic market-state estimation, technical indicators, volatility measures, momentum metrics, market structure information, pattern-recognition signals and hybrid features. Experiments were conducted using approximately eleven years of minute-level market data spanning multiple market regimes. Multiple reward formulations, random seeds and evaluation environments were employed to assess robustness. The results provide strong evidence that richer state representations improve the quality of learned trading policies. The engineered representation consistently generated substantially greater gross profitability and superior frictionless performance compared to the Raw OHLC baseline. However, net profitability after accounting for realistic transaction costs remained negative for both representations under most tested configurations, indicating that improvements in signal quality have not yet translated into deployable profitability. Furthermore, the study identified a previously unreported interaction between state representation complexity and reward-function design, referred to as State-Reward Alignment. Experimental results demonstrate that richer state representations may fail under poorly aligned reward structures while significantly outperforming simpler representations when paired with sufficiently informative reward signals. Feature-audit analysis further revealed a dominance of probabilistic state-estimation features among the strongest predictive signals within the engineered representation. In particular, a novel hybrid feature, the Pattern-Conditioned Probability of Upward Movement, ranked fourth among all 89 evaluated features, providing preliminary evidence that combining Markov transition probabilities with pattern-recognition information may offer meaningful predictive value. Collectively, the findings support the hypotheses that richer state representations provide superior learning environments for reinforcementlearning trading agents and that reward-function sophistication must increase alongside state complexity to fully realize this advantage. These results suggest that the joint design of state representations and reward functions represents a critical direction for future research in financial reinforcement learning.
why: RL trading with 89-dim states; competent but forgettable.

title: Pricing Managerial Sentiment
abstract: We investigate whether the managerial sentiment expressed in corporate disclosures consists of systematic pricing information that extends beyond what is captured by traditional accounting and price-based factors. We rely on a comprehensive panel of Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) sections obtained from S&P 500 firms for the period 2015-2025 and score sentiment at the sentence level by using a financial domain-trained language model. We reveal that future stock returns are strongly and consistently associated with changes in managerial caution, while higher levels of managerial optimism are associated with subsequent underperformance. We also reveal that these relationships are asymmetric, concentrated, and nonlinear; moreover, they lie in the tails of the return distribution. These findings indicate that disclosures are most informative when changes in managerial sentiment are extreme. On this basis, we construct a zero-cost managerial sentiment factor, ToneF, that goes long on firms that exhibit large changes in caution and short on firms whose management exhibits increased levels of optimism levels. ToneF earns a positive and statistically significant return premium, exhibits low volatility, and is not characterized by any meaningful autocorrelation. We use spanning regressions to reveal that ToneF is not spanned by the Fama-French five factors or the momentum factor and that it retains a significant intercept, thus suggesting that it captures an independent dimension of priced information. Changes in 2 managerial sentiment at the firm level explain economically meaningful variation in future returns. At the portfolio level, we reveal that augmenting the FF5+MOM model with ToneF leads to a systematic reduction in pricing errors and an increase in explanatory power for portfolios sorted on managerial sentiment.
why: MD&A sentiment predicts returns; no costs or OOS detail.

title: A Three-Factor Hull-White Scenario Generator for Macro-Financial Stress Forecasting
abstract: This paper builds a scenario engine that maps a yield-curve path into a distribution of macro-financial outcomes. A three-factor Hull-White model generates arbitrage-free curves whose factors are simulated under the physical measure, with an estimated and reported market price of risk. A Minnesota-prior VARX maps the simulated curves into weekly equity returns, the federal funds rate, the Weekly Economic Index, inflation and a bank Marginal Expected Shortfall proxy, with a sign-restricted policy shock adapted to weekly data. Evaluated out of sample from 2017 to 2024, the term-structure block has the lowest forecast error in 13 of 20 maturity and horizon cells, and the density forecasts are well calibrated for the continuously moving variables. At weekly frequency the curve carries no incremental information about these variables once their own lags are controlled for, so the engine's value lies in conditioning on a specified curve path, which no benchmark can do.
why: Hull-White stress scenario engine; out-of-sample, null result.

title: Not All Inflation Is Equally Predictable: Machine Learning Evidence Across Countries and Price Categories
abstract: Can machine learning improve short-horizon inflation forecasts across countries and price concepts? We compare sixteen statistical and machine learning algorithms with five simple benchmarks for headline, food, energy/housing-proxy, core, and producer inflation. The source panel contains 189 economies; audited index and history requirements yield test samples of 64 to 171 economies. Models forecast one new monthly log price change and reconstruct year-on-year inflation from eleven known monthly changes. Initial estimation uses 1995-2013, baseline selection uses 2014-2017, and annual expanding evaluations cover 2018-2023. The original validation-selected ensembles reduce country-balanced loss relative to persistence by approximately 21-27 percent. They outperform the selected simple benchmark for the four consumer measures, but the selected full-information producer model does not establish an advantage over a pooled autoregression. The external macroeconomic/global block improves on own-plus-cross-inflation inputs only for headline and core inflation. Review-stage extensions examine expanding validation, country-balanced and annual-loss-aligned fitting, factor and heterogeneous-country benchmarks, forecast combinations, delayed non-own inputs, quantile-trained forecasts, denominator leverage, and conditional instability. These extensions are not an untouched confirmation sample. Expanding validation preserves the five within-family choices. A producer forecast combination improves point loss over a pooled twelve-lag ridge autoregression (AR12) without establishing a statistically significant advantage. Quantile-trained models lower matched asymmetric loss, although coverage and extreme-error limitations remain. The results concern revised historical data: they do not reconstruct historical releases, vintages, or series availability, and therefore do not establish historical real-time operational accuracy.
why: Cross-country ML inflation forecasts; out-of-sample but macro.

title: Frontier Technology in Frontier Markets? Financing Global AI Entrepreneurship
abstract: Does the global diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) extend to the creation and financing of the firms that build it? Using a novel dataset of 116,795 startups founded between 2015 and 2022 across 172 countries, we link company descriptions and financing histories to the employment and education records of founders, early employees, and potential investors. We document a stark divergence between the real and financial sides of global AI entrepreneurship. On the real side, AI startups everywhere display the hallmarks of a general-purpose technology: in every world region, they target more customer sectors than comparable non-AI startups and are more likely to sell horizontal products that apply across industries. Moreover, following the release of ChatGPT, startups whose baseline tasks were more amenable to AI expanded the breadth of their work activities and commercial staffing. Yet the financing advantage that such scalable businesses command is sharply localized. AI startups raise 151 percent more annual capital than non-AI peers in North America and 181 percent more in the Middle East, compared with 42 percent more in East Asia, 16 percent more in Europe, and no detectable premium in Africa, Latin America, or South Asia. Accounting for targeted customer markets, founder credentials, early-team human capital, and local investor characteristics explains part of the gap in Latin America but leaves the broader global divide intact. In Africa, half of all AI funding goes to basic compute and data-center infrastructure; excluding these providers reveals that African AI product startups raise 57 percent less than non-AI peers. These patterns provide an early warning that AI may reach users around the world without building firms around the world.
why: Global AI startup financing dataset; not next-week actionable.

title: Stablecoin Runs as Safe-Asset Stress Signals: Episode-Level Evidence for Central Bank Surveillance
abstract: This paper asks whether stablecoin runs carry information about U.S. Treasury yields. Using daily data on USDT, USDC and BUSD from 2021 to 2025 and five stress episodes, it measures flows from changes in token units rather than market capitalisation, which removes the phantom inflows the standard measure records when tokens lose their peg. Flows have no stable relationship with yields in normal periods. During the three panic-driven runs, a one-billion-dollar five-day redemption is associated with an 8.5 basis point fall in the three-month bill yield within ten trading days, while two regulatory episodes carry no such signal. The response is broad across maturities and has the opposite sign to what reserve liquidation predicts, which points to flight to quality. The effect is led by the TerraUSD collapse and corroborated by the USDC/SVB run. Five-day redemptions of roughly USD 2 to 3 billion during a panic mark the scale at which stablecoin stress becomes informative for surveillance.
why: Stablecoin runs signal Treasury yields; episode-level macro.

title: Algorithmic Scrutiny and the Pricing of Machine Narratives: An Agent-Based Model of Artificial Intelligence and IPO Outcomes in China's Automotive Industry
abstract: Chinese automakers and intelligent-driving suppliers increasingly go public on the strength of artificial intelligence narratives, while the investors who price these offerings increasingly rely on artificial intelligence to read them. We develop an agent-based model of the initial public offering (IPO) process in which founders decide whether to persist toward listing, institutional investors with human or algorithmic analytics bid in bookbuilding, retail investors respond to media sentiment, and prices converge on intrinsic value over the following year. Virtual experiments on 600 heterogeneous cohorts comprising 116,623 simulated listings yield seven propositions. Institutional adoption of AI analytics lowers initial returns monotonically, yet pricing error is U-shaped in adoption because attention-triggered scrutiny overcorrects narrativeheavy issuers and homogeneous models correlate errors across a cohort. Positive media sentiment has an inverted U-shaped relationship with the aftermarket valuation premium, and AI adoption shifts the turning point toward lower sentiment. Approval-based valuation caps tax AIintensive issuers disproportionately. AI calibration of founder persistence raises the value created by a listing cohort and cuts post-IPO public-to-private reversals, but a novelty penalty in calibration tools screens out viable AI-native ventures. The model integrates signaling, narrative, and imprinting perspectives with a view of AI as both an information technology and an entrepreneurial actor.
why: China auto IPO agent-based simulation; no implementation path.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI in Asset Management Large Language Models, Autonomous Agents and the Information Efficiency of Equity Markets
abstract: This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, in particular large language models (LLMs) and autonomous AI agents, changes the information efficiency of equity markets and the practice of asset management, and how it differs from the classical quantitative models of systematic investing. Building on Fama (1970) and Grossman and Stiglitz (1980), we argue that generative AI lowers the cost of processing unstructured information rather than the cost of acquiring private information, so that its first-order effect is a faster incorporation of public text into prices and a shortening of post-announcement drifts. We review the empirical literature from the dictionary methods of Loughran and McDonald (2011) to the LLM-based return-prediction studies of Lopez-Lira and Tang (2023) and Chen, Kelly and Xiu (2022), and we set out a complete research design for an event study of AI-based sentiment measures and price reactions to earnings calls of blue-chip stocks. Applications are discussed separately for funds and for individual mandates, with documented examples from practice.
why: Generative AI asset management position paper; no results yet.

title: Trading Before a Committed Rebalance
abstract: An institution must complete a portfolio adjustment, but traders who prepare inventory for it can choose whether to participate. We study how public forecasts affect the institution's cost in a Bayesian execution game with optional activation, transient impact, and uniform-price terminal completion. The curvature of equilibrium cost as a function of the posterior target mean determines the value of information. In the scalar model, information benefits every fixed participation roster. Optional supply can reverse this ranking at entry, at full participation, and in a smooth interior with lognormal activation costs. For centered scalar targets, information weakly lowers cost relative to no information, strictly when the posterior mean is nonzero with positive probability. Centered Gaussian precision gains are always beneficial. An exact symmetric finite-population equilibrium identifies how information resolution and individual strategic size interact near entry. A portfolio extension gives a matrix criterion for the fixed-roster ranking, which can fail under general cross-impact. Even with isotropic execution, shared activation allows equally accurate signals about target magnitude and composition to have opposite execution values under one unchanged prior. Intraday ETF price data is used to characterize target uncertainty and trading conditions without identifying activation or institutional costs.
why: Execution game theory; no data or implementation path.

title: Neckpinches in a Positively Curved Market: Ricci Flow with Surgery on the Nikkei-225
abstract: We study the intrinsic geometry of the Nikkei-225 through the discrete Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC) of its empirical correlation graph, using the graph Ricci flow and surgery methodology of arXiv:2510.15942. The 226-node correlation graph, built from daily returns between January 2020 and June 2026, is ORC-spherical: every edge has strictly positive curvature before any flow, close to the equal-weight value $κ\approx0.502$. Under a fixed 20-iteration Ricci flow the curvature distribution polarises into a high-curvature bulk and a low-curvature minority, and cutting the low-curvature edges splits the graph into components of 184 and 42 nodes. The recursive ARCUS procedure (Adaptive Ricci Curvature Unsupervised Surgery) stops the flow at each node once a curvature gap ratio $G$ exceeds $G_{\min}$ and the surgery set is stable. With $G_{\min}=10$ and a minimum cluster size of 15, ARCUS performs 28 surgeries over 13 levels and ends in 29 terminal clusters of 2-14 nodes. The stopping rule fires at every node, with $G$ between 10.0 and 92.4, and the top-level split reproduces the fixed-schedule 184/42 partition exactly. Eight small subgraphs stop with $G<15$, so the deeper levels are conditional on $G_{\min}$. Many terminal clusters are single industries by inspection, among them nine banks, five insurers, five general trading companies, three steelmakers and three shipping lines. Two delisted stocks without price data enter as zero-correlation placeholders; with them excluded, every terminal cluster is more strongly correlated internally than with the rest of the index.
why: Ricci curvature on Nikkei graph; no trading baseline.

title: Bond yield dynamics: a multi-country multi-horizon string model
abstract: This article extends the forward rate curve model of Baaquie and Bouchaud (2004) and Le Coz and Bouchaud (2024) to the multi-country setting of government bond markets. Cross-country blocks of correlation matrices of realized yield changes are found to display significant asymmetry between maturities. In the framework of the proposed model, this amounts to give to each country an idiosyncratic time scale. Each time scale describes how the perceived time between future dates depends on the dates themselves. The differences between these time scales structure the interactions between curves and reproduce the characteristic asymmetry of cross-country correlation matrices. The proposed model captures the full set of cross-curve correlations simultaneously at both daily and intra-day frequencies. When calibrated on government bonds issued by nine countries of the euro-zone, the typical reconstruction error is 1.7%.
why: Multi-country bond yield string model; calibration only.

title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
abstract: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.
why: Generative engine optimization network mapping, marginal finance

title: Digital Banking and Economic Growth in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review of Financial Inclusion and Innovation
abstract: This study examines digital banking transformation in Bangladesh, with particular emphasis on financial inclusion, economic growth, Mobile Financial Services (MFS), financial technology (fintech), Artificial Intelligence (AI), smart banking, and barriers to inclusive development. Methodology: A systematic review searched Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language studies (2015-2025) on digital, internet, online, mobile, e-banking, and financial inclusion. From 58 articles, 35 peer-reviewed papers met predefined criteria following deduplication, quality assessment, and full-text analysis. Results: Digital banking expands access, lowers operating/transaction costs, and speeds services, indirectly supporting inclusion, entrepreneurship, SME finance, investment, and employment. However, technological, human, economic, social, institutional, security, and trust barriers including connectivity, skills, affordability, cyberthreats, privacy, regulatory uncertainty, and rural-urban disparities limit benefits. Conclusions: Sustainable transformation requires coordinated progress in infrastructure, skills development, cost management, regulation, cybersecurity, consumer protection, and equitable access beyond technology. Limitations: This review is limited by database coverage, publication bias, methodological heterogeneity, and restricted access to full-text articles, which may reduce the comprehensiveness and generalizability of the evidence. Contributions: This research integrates economic growth, technological development, and challenges into an inclusive framework explaining Bangladesh's transition toward broadbased, intelligent banking.
why: Survey of Bangladesh digital banking; single-country review.

title: Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Expertocracy Digitalization: AI-Amplified Credit Risk & Uncertainty Rating Techno-Managerialism
abstract: Workplace analyses frequently depict digitalization and artificial intelligence (AI) organizational incorporation as disruptive, optimizing, or democratizing. Despite extensive studies of AI's transformative labour configurations, more obscure is how financial AI-mediated techno-managerialism stabilizes professional relationships, revitalizes expert authority, and suppresses organizational change. Problematizing precarious, cross-occupational (sovereign) credit risk management sociomaterial digitalization, I reveal how credit rating agency (CRA) and investor algorithmic/automated decision-making (ADM) promotes institutional stasis: (technological) innovation without (relational) transformation. Taken for granted and virtually unaccountable, repeatedly, enterprise AI-machine learning (ML) amplification of reflexive professional technoscientific rating generates and reinforces CRA-investor interorganizational convergence. Accelerated and scaled-up, AI/ADM-inherited, geometrics-driven 'debt sustainability analysis' (DSA) and calculative infrastructure deepen industrywide interdependence. Deconstruction/reconstruction of prevailing CRA and investor hybrid 'default risk/uncertainty' DSA techno-managerial modalities reveals synergistic sociotechnical rating methods digitalization ill-informs fixed-income futurity financialization. Advancing sustainable management/OS through economic sociology, I analyze market ADM/AI-assimilated ratings 'expertocracy' - knowledge-based expert rule - (re)validation of tenuous interorganizational conditions and professional affinities. Commercial AI-ML CRA-investor alignment breathes new, automated scale into legacy DSAs, (re)enacting a crisis-prone (neoliberal) political economy of creditworthiness (PEC) referential/data infrastructure 'inertia'. I study scores Passive/Active investor (reflexive) professional performance and (AI/ADM-intensified) analytical, organizational, and normative CRA correspondence reinforcing relations. Magnifying global (corporate) expertocracy, national democracy, and environmental imbalances, sociotechnical PEC interlinkages (re)embed a self-systemic/self-regulating digitalization dominance, diminishing capacities for sustainable twin transition.
why: Sociomaterial credit risk theory; no data or implementation.

title: Financial Innovation Segmentations: Overview Of Concepts, Theories, Opportunities, Challenges And Future Research
abstract: This article explores the recent financial innovation segmentations in the financial system, their objectives, benefits, interrelationship, challenges, and risks. This article contributes to the literature by exploring how these advancements facilitate risk mitigation and efficient financial intermediation. It highlights the theories and types of financial innovation segmentation in the financial system, which includes open banking, open finance, embedded finance, decentralised finance, cryptocurrency, central bank digital currencies (CBDC), stablecoins, Fintech, artificial intelligence finance, sustainable finance (ESG finance), red finance, black finance, blue finance, social finance, blended finance, RegTech, and SupTech. Several areas for future research are suggested.
why: Financial innovation taxonomy overview; position/review paper.

title: Statistical moments, risk weighting and percentiles of a loss distribution of a finite homogeneous credit portfolio; extending the Vasicek distribution
abstract: The Vasicek distribution assumes an infinite portfolio of identical obligors and forms the basis of the Basel III/IV Risk Weighted Assets (RWA) calculation. We derive the central moments of the loss distribution for a finite number (n) of obligors. We use these moments to calculate percentiles of the fraction (x) of defaulted obligors, via the Cornish-Fisher expansion and via a weighting method. Both methods are based on scaling the standard deviation in x by a capital multiple. The weighting method assumes that the capital multiple is linear in the central moments and leads to an Extended Vasicek distribution. We apply this distribution in calculating an adjusted RWA for small portfolios. Simulations show that this adjustment is only relevant for small portfolios of less than 100 obligors and that the Extended Vasicek distribution allows analytical risk capital calculations for portfolios with different rating grades, even when the number of obligors per rating grade is small.
why: Finite-credit Vasicek extension; pure theory, no data.

title: Feasible sub-replicating portfolios for basket options via the block rearrangement algorithm
abstract: We construct sub-replicating portfolios of vanilla options for a basket call when the marginal distributions of the underlying assets are known and their dependence is not. To do so, we reduce the n-asset problem to n two-asset problems of the type solved by Hobson, Laurence, and Wang (2005a), and use the Block Rearrangement Algorithm1 (BRA) to approximate the minimising dependence among the assets. The cash component of the portfolio is computed exactly, so that its price is a valid lower bound, and reassembling the BRA output with the original marginals gives an upper bound computed by quadrature; together they bracket the minimum basket-option price. In log-normal examples with three and six assets the bracket has a relative width of at most 0.1%, and the corresponding sub-replicating portfolios are sparse, using only two strikes per asset, while the resulting bounds are tighter than those obtained from a general-purpose multi-marginal optimal-transport algorithm with strikes on a grid. We also give the lower bound and an optimal portfolio in closed form in three special cases: a deep in-the-money basket, a basket with one dominant asset, and jointly mixable marginals.
why: Basket option replication bounds; pure derivatives theory.

title: Equity and Aggregate Ambiguity
abstract: Equitable resource allocations in the context of symmetric risk exposures are intuitively desirable and sometimes even expected in public planning. However, public planners generally are also concerned with mitigating risk and, more generally, uncertainty and ambiguity. We study a fundamental conflict between equity and ambiguity avoidance in public risk allocation problems. Our main results are framed and established in the setting of general symmetric aggregate losses equipped with dependence uncertainty among individual losses. Specializing to the classical model of Keeney (1980), we prove that an increase in equity is equivalent to an increase in aggregate ambiguity. We then provide a quantitative characterization of equity and ambiguity avoidance through the $α$-maxmin preference framework, establishing conditions on ambiguity and risk attitudes under which each criterion holds. Specifically, equity corresponds to ambiguity or risk proneness, while ambiguity avoidance corresponds to ambiguity or risk aversion. The analysis extends to general classes of symmetric aggregation functions, where we show that ambiguity attitude is the primary determinant of preference, though aggregation structure and risk attitude also play important roles. Numerical illustrations validate our theoretical findings and explore the equity-ambiguity tradeoff.
why: Equity-ambiguity theory; no data or implementation.

title: Optimal Control in Pairs Trading with Negative-Power Utility
abstract: We solve a finite-horizon consumption and investment problem in a pairs trading model with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck spread and utility $U(x)=-x^{-γ}$, $γ>0$. Linearizing the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation gives explicit formulas for the value function and the optimal feedback control. A budget inequality and concavity verify optimality over all admissible strategies with nonnegative wealth on every finite horizon, without Novikov's condition. Under the optimal feedback, wealth and consumption admit deterministic upper bounds when the interest rate $r$ is at most the mean-reversion rate $κ$. If $r>κ$, each exceeds any prescribed level with positive probability at every time after the start. If $r>\sqrt{2+γ} κ$, there is an explicit critical horizon at and beyond which expected terminal wealth is infinite, while optimal expected utility is finite. When the critical time falls before maturity, expected wealth at that time is finite exactly when the initial spread is zero. We also show that the suprema of the negative powers of optimal wealth and consumption are integrable on every finite horizon exactly for orders $0<m\le 1+γ$.
why: Pairs trading optimal control; theory without data.

title: Disentangling Monitor Hardware Artifacts and Smoothing Lag for Shift-Robust Intraoperative EEG and Hemodynamic Risk Calibration
abstract: Commercial intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) and blood pressure monitors introduce cyclic impedance pulses, smoothing delays, direct-current (DC) drift, and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration. We developed a causal signal-conditioning and shift-robust conformal calibration framework across 5,439 public anesthesia procedures. Streaming filters blank 10.13-min 64-Hz impedance checks, apply unclipped post-notch conditioning, separate 63-s suppression-ratio lag, and distinguish three-channel cuff inflations from dropouts across propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA; N = 3,214), volatile anesthesia (N = 2,046), European endoscopy sedation (N = 171), and DC-coupled surgery (N = 8). De-impedanced cortical tree ensembles were compared against deep sequence models, paired with patient-cluster Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control (CRC) and lag-buffered online Conformal Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) tracking. Pre-filter blanking removed 97.90% and 97.60% of false flatline conflicts while preserving 99.23% and 98.96% of deep suppression. On unseen TIVA surgeries (N = 525), cortical features achieved area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) 0.3135 (1.94% prevalence) and 0.1627 (0.82% lag-free prevalence), with no detectable difference from deep encoders (p >= 0.36) and no cortical gain for hypotension (0.3432 vs. 0.3437, p = 0.784). Zero-retraining volatile transfer (N = 1,048) showed no detectable difference from an end-tidal gas oracle on lag-free suppression (0.0820 vs. 0.0736, p = 0.472). Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted CRC bounded all 70 TIVA shift cells at <= 4.38% (alpha = 5.0%) in 66.32 ms per 30-s epoch. Causal artifact disentangling and shift-aware conformal calibration support reliable real-time intraoperative risk bounds within explicit physiological observability limits.
why: Anesthesia monitoring; off-topic for finance.

title: Scalable fault vulnerability analysis for ReRAM-based process-in-memory CNN accelerators
abstract: Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM)-based processing-in-memory (PIM) accelerators offer a highly efficient platform for parallel matrix-vector multiplications (VMM) in neural networks, leveraging analog computation, high density, low leakage, and non-volatility. However, their susceptibility to permanent faults, such as stuck-at-high (\textit{SaH}) and stuck-at-low (\textit{SaL}) resistance states, permanently corrupts the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) weights mapped onto ReRAM cell conductance values, thereby degrading inference accuracy and leading to system unreliability in safety-critical applications. Fault injection is a commonly used technique to assess the vulnerability of neural networks by systematically injecting faults into individual parameters and measuring the resulting accuracy degradation. Although this method is accurate, it is prohibitively time-consuming and computationally expensive, especially for large-scale CNNs. In this paper, we propose a fast, scalable, and analytical framework to quantify the fault vulnerability of convolutional neural networks deployed on ReRAM-based PIM accelerators. This method quantifies vulnerability at different granularities, including weights, kernels, and layers, without the need for exhaustive simulation, enabling the design of fault-tolerant accelerators for edge and safety-critical applications. The comparison between the results of the proposed vulnerability score (VS) metrics with performance metric of CNNs captured with fault injection simulations confirms the effectiveness of our proposed method. Unlike exhaustive fault injection, which requires days or weeks, whereas the proposed approach achieves a speedup of about $10^4\times-10^5\times$, enabling fast and accurate vulnerability analysis for large-scale CNNs within only a few minutes or hours.
why: ReRAM accelerator fault analysis; off-topic hardware.
